# Mechanical clock (escapement, spring drive) (`mechanical_clock`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/physics.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Physics, optics & astronomy (`physics`)
- Deps: needs gears_gear_trains; helped by wire_drawing, lathe_screw_cutting
- Core idea: A falling weight on a cord turns a train of gears; an escapement lets the train advance only one tooth at a time, so the weight runs down in steps instead of crashing. In the verge escapement a crown wheel with saw teeth pushes two small plates (pallets) on an upright rod alternately; the rod carries a crossbar with movable weights (foliot) or a wheel (balance) that swings to and fro and sets the rate. Such clocks err by a quarter of an hour a day or more and are set by a sundial. A coiled steel spring instead of the weight makes the clock portable; a cone-shaped fusee evens out the spring's weakening pull. Real accuracy comes only with the pendulum (1656) and the balance spring (1675).
- Pitfalls:
  - Describing gears and hands but no escapement; that is the whole invention
  - Jumping straight to a pendulum or a watch without the metalworking (hardened steel springs, cut pinions)
  - Promising minute accuracy from a verge and foliot
  - Calling Henlein the inventor of the watch (small spring clocks existed before him)
- History: china: 725 Yi Xing and Liang Lingzan's water-driven armillary with a stop-release linkage; 1088–1094 Su Song's astronomical clock tower, Kaifeng; islamic: 11th c. al-Muradi's geared water clocks; 1206 al-Jazari's automata clocks; c. 1560 Taqi al-Din describes weight and spring clocks; europe: c. 1270–1300 weight-driven verge clock (Dunstable 1283 is the first likely record); 1364 de Dondi's Astrarium; c. 1430 spring drive and fusee; c. 1500–1510 portable watches in Nuremberg and Italy; 1675 balance spring (Huygens; Hooke claims priority)
- Read:
  - David S. Landes, Revolution in Time (1983)
  - Joseph Needham, Wang Ling & Derek J. de Solla Price, Heavenly Clockwork (1960)
  - Carlo M. Cipolla, Clocks and Culture 1300–1700 (1967)
